newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arafat in Egypt ahead of Egypt-Israel summit.
newsitem.headline: Arafat in Egypt ahead of Egypt-Israel summit.

text.p: A summit between Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to revive Middle East peacemaking faces the formidable obstacle of entrenched differences over Jewish settlement of Arab land.
Mubarak held talks on Monday in the Egyptian capital with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. The two leaders often consult on the deadlocked peace process.
"All hopes are pinned on the Sharm el-Sheikh meeting," Egypt's al-Akhbar newspaper said in an editorial in advance of Tuesday's summit.
An Israeli diplomat in Cairo agreed: "We hope that this summit will enable us to get out of the current situation to the benefit of all sides to achieve full and comprehensive peace."
The issue of Jewish settlement on Palestinian lands captured in 1967 is looming over the summit planned for the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Sharm el-Sheikh. There is no sign of compromise.

"The meeting will be a crossroads. Either the beginning of a denouement or leaving matters to get worse," an Arab analyst said of the fourth meeting between Mubarak and Netanyahu since the rightwing Israeli took office in June 1996.
Mediator Egypt supports the Palestinian view that they will only resume talks when Israel halts work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
But Netanyahu told Israel Army Radio after being asked about reports of a possible settlement freeze: "It is not on the agenda -- not on mine."

Palestinian-Israeli peacemaking was halted in March when Israel started building the settlement of Har Homa in East Jerusalem. Israel captured the area in 1967 but its subsequent annexation was not recognised by most countries.

Palestinians see the work at the site they call Jabal Abu Ghneim as pre-empting final status talks on the east of the city, which they see as the capital of a future state. Israel says the entire city is its capital.
"I think the key...will be settlements and Judaisation," said Saeed Kamal, assistant secretary general for Palestinian affairs at the Arab League.

"The punchline is a formula in which the Israelis have to accept freezing settlements in Har Homa," an Arab analyst said. "This is a critical meeting in which the Israelis should come up with an acceptance of freezing."

Egypt's Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said in broadcast remarks on Friday the summit would succeed if Israel agreed to stop building settlements. Mubarak said in Germany last week a six-month suspension of Jewish settlement building could restart the peace process.
"The hope is that if they accept a moratorium or temporary freeze on settlements, then the new momentum will force the peace process out of a rut," the analyst said.

That hope looks unlikely -- a view underlined by Israel predicting the summit would make limited progress on ending the crisis and Mubarak saying on Saturday he had sent envoy Osama al-Baz to Israel to prepare for the summit without any preconditions.
"Israel has not offered to stop work on the Har Homa neighbourhood. We are not proposing it," Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said.
